passages.title: Manners before Allah and His Messenger
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open the sūrah by teaching the believers the manners they owe to Allah and to His Messenger ﷺ — three concrete etiquettes: do not run ahead of him (ayah 1), do not raise your voice over his (ayat 2–3), and do not shout for him at his door (ayat 4–5). What holds them together is a single insight: the ordinary rules of conversation do not apply to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As Ibn Kathir puts it, in these ayat Allah teaches His faithful servants the good manners they should observe with the Messenger ﷺ — respect, honour and esteem.

## The background of revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Qurtubi that six separate narratives are cited as the background of these verses, and that Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn ʿArabi confirmed that all of them are correct, because they all fall inside the general meaning of the verses. The sources before us set out two of those scenes, and both involve a delegation from the tribe of Banu Tamim who came to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah.

**The first scene: a disagreement that grew loud.** Al-Bukhari records that a delegation from Banu Tamim came to the Prophet ﷺ, and that Abu Bakr proposed Al-Qaʿqaʿ bin Maʿbad to be appointed as their leader while ʿUmar proposed Al-Aqraʿ bin Habis. Abu Bakr said to ʿUmar, "You only wanted to contradict me," and ʿUmar answered, "I did not intend to contradict you." Al-Bukhari also records from Ibn Abi Mulaykah what happened next: **"The two righteous ones, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, almost earned destruction when they raised their voices before the Prophet ﷺ"** — who was at that moment receiving the delegation of Banu Tamim. Ibn Kathir notes that it was stated that ayah 2 was revealed about Abu Bakr and ʿUmar.

**The second scene: men shouting at a curtain.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Imam Baghawi, on the authority of Qatadah, that the Banu Tamim delegation reached Madinah in the afternoon and came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was resting in one of his apartments. These bedouins were not acquainted with the manners and etiquette of settled society. They stood outside the apartment and called out: *O Muhammad, come out to us!* Ayah 4 was revealed on that occasion. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Musnad of Ahmad, Tirmidhi and others record similar reports with differing wordings, as quoted by Mazhari.)

The finest of the Companions and the roughest of the bedouins are both being taught — because reverence for the Messenger ﷺ is not a matter of refinement or temperament. It has to be learned.

## Ayah 1: "Do not proceed ahead"

**The phrase.** *Bayna yadayi* literally means "between the two hands," but in Arabic usage, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, it simply means "in front of" or "ahead of." So: do not go ahead of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

**The silence is the point.** Notice what the ayah does *not* say: ahead of him *in what*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the Qur'an does not specify the matter, so the prohibition appears general — it covers going ahead by word and by deed alike. Wait for the Messenger's ﷺ reply rather than answering for him, unless he himself appoints someone to reply. If he is walking, no one should overtake him. If people are sitting at a meal, no one should start eating before him. And where there is clear indication or strong evidence that he himself wants someone sent forward, that is different — some people used to be asked to go on a journey or an expedition ahead of him.

**What Ibn Kathir draws out.** He glosses it as: do not rush in making decisions before him; rather, follow his lead in all matters. Two early comments sharpen this. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported that **Ibn ʿAbbas** explained it as, *"Do not say anything that contradicts the Qur'an and Sunnah."* And **Qatadah** commented, "We were told that some people used to say, 'Revelation should be sent down about such and such matters,' and, 'such and such practices should be rendered allowed.' Allah the Exalted disliked this attitude."

That second comment is the sharpest edge of the ayah. There is a way of speaking about religion in which a person is quietly legislating — deciding in advance what the ruling *ought* to be, then expecting revelation to catch up. The ayah forbids that posture at the root.

**"And have taqwā of Allah. Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing."** *Taqwā* is the carefulness that keeps a servant inside the bounds his Lord has set. Ibn Kathir reads the closing pair precisely: *Hearing* — your statements; *Knowing* — your intentions. Adab has an outward half and an inward half, and each is met by a divine name that misses nothing. Taqwā here, he says, means taqwā in what Allah has ordered you.

## Ayat 2–3: the voice

Ayah 2 forbids two distinct things. The first is *raising your voices above the voice of the Prophet* ﷺ — a matter of volume and precedence, drowning him out. The second is *speaking aloud to him in talk as you speak aloud to one another* — a matter of manner: addressing him in the same blunt, casual register you use with a peer. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah prohibited speaking to the Prophet ﷺ in a loud voice, as one speaks loudly to another in a way that offends him; instead they were required to speak to him in terms of respect, honour and calmness. He links the ayah to Allah's words elsewhere: *"Make not the calling of the Messenger among you as your calling one of another"* (24:63).

**"Lest your deeds should be thwarted while you perceive not."** Ibn Kathir explains the warning: you were ordered to refrain from raising your voices to the Prophet ﷺ so that he would not get angry with you, because in doing so you also anger Allah — and the good deeds of the one who caused the Prophet's ﷺ anger become useless without his even knowing it. He then notes that in the Sahih there is a hadith that states: *"Verily, a man might utter a word that pleases Allah the Exalted, even though he does not recognise the significance of his word, and on its account Paradise is written for him. Verily, a man might utter a word carelessly that angers Allah the Exalted, and on its account he is cast in the Fire farther than the distance between the heavens and earth."*

**How the Companions received it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when this verse was revealed the blessed Companions became very apprehensive and very cautious. Abu Bakr said, "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, from now till my last breath I shall speak to you as if someone is whispering" (Ad-Durr-ul-Manthur, on the authority of Baihaqi). And ʿUmar's voice became so low that the Prophet ﷺ had to ask him to repeat what he said in order to understand him — a report Ibn Kathir gives from ʿAbdullah bin Az-Zubayr, who did not mention the same regarding his own father, Abu Bakr.

**Thabit bin Qays.** The most moving case is a man whose voice was simply loud by nature. Al-Bukhari records from Anas bin Malik that the Prophet ﷺ missed Thabit bin Qays, and a man said, "O Allah's Messenger! I will find out about his news." He went and found Thabit sitting at home with his head lowered, and asked, "What is the matter?" — "An evil matter!" He said that he used to raise his voice above the voice of the Prophet ﷺ, and he feared that his good deeds would be useless and that he would be among the people of the Fire. The man carried the news back, and returned to Thabit with wonderfully good news; the Prophet ﷺ had said: *"Go back to him and tell him this news; you are not among the people of the Fire. Rather, you are among the dwellers of Paradise."*

Imam Ahmad's narration from Anas adds the ending, with the Prophet's ﷺ words there given as *"Nay, he is among the dwellers of Paradise."* Anas said, "We used to see Thabit walk among us knowing that he was to be among the dwellers of Paradise." Then during the battle of Yamamah, when the Muslim forces suffered retreat, Thabit bin Qays bin Shammas came forward having already put on his *hanut* — the perfume used for the dead — and his shrouds, and said, "The worst habit is the one you acquire from your enemy, and do not set a bad example for your companions." He went on fighting until he was martyred.

## The hard question in ayah 2

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a genuine difficulty.

According to the unanimous view of Ahl-us-Sunnah wal-Jamāʿah, the only thing that can destroy righteous deeds is *kufr* — disbelief. No sin destroys good deeds. Yet here the Qur'an addresses the noble Companions and the believers as *"O you who believe"* — which shows that they are believers, not disbelievers. How, then, can their righteous works be spoken of as rendered void? And there is a second problem: faith is an act of free will, and so is disbelief — no one becomes a disbeliever unless he adopts it by his own free will. But the ayah says *"while you perceive not,"* which sounds like a punishment falling on someone unawares.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the resolution of its author's teacher in *Bayan-ul-Qur'an*. The ayah warns of a *danger*, a chain that could begin here. Raising one's voice above the Prophet's ﷺ is tantamount to discourtesy toward him, which is the same as vexing him. It is unthinkable that the noble Companions would intentionally attempt to hurt him — but actions such as "advancing forward" and "raising voices" can upset or offend without any intention to offend. So all such conduct has been absolutely prohibited, forbidden, and regarded as sin. Now, some sins have this character: those who commit them lose the divine aid of repentance and the capacity to perform righteous works, become so engrossed in sin that it leads them to disbelief — at which point the righteous deeds fail. And because the believer may never have intended to cause hurt in the first place, he would not even perceive how he became involved in that process. That is the force of *"while you perceive not."*

The same source adds that some scholars extended this warning: someone who takes a righteous, holy person as his spiritual guide and then shows disrespect to him may suffer the same consequences — divine aid removed, and the treasure of faith itself destroyed. We seek refuge with Allah from it.

## Ayah 3: the reward for lowering the voice

Having forbidden, Allah now praises. *Verily, those who lower their voices in the presence of Allah's Messenger, they are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for taqwā. For them is forgiveness and a great reward.* Ibn Kathir explains "tested for taqwā" as hearts that Allah has purified and made a residence and dwelling for taqwā — not merely visited by taqwā, but lived in by it.

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad, in the *Book of Az-Zuhd*, that Mujahid said someone wrote to ʿUmar: "O Leader of the faithful! Who is better, a man who does not feel the desire to commit a sin and does not commit it, or a man who feels the desire to commit a sin but does not commit it?" ʿUmar replied: "He who feels desire to commit a sin, but does not commit it — *they are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for taqwā. For them is forgiveness and a great reward.*" Taqwā, on this reading, is not the absence of a pull. It is what a heart does with the pull.

Note also that the ayah moves from *the Prophet* in ayah 2 to *the Messenger of Allah* in ayah 3 — and that the restraint it praises is the exact reverse of the failure it has just described. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah, having forbidden the one, then ordains lowering one's voice before the Messenger ﷺ and encourages, directs and recommends this better behaviour.

## Ayat 4–5: shouting at the door

**The apartments.** *Hujurāt* is the plural of *hujrah*: lexically, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, a four-walled apartment or dwelling comprising a courtyard and a roofed building. In Madinah the Prophet ﷺ had nine wives, each with her own separate apartment, and he used to stay with them in succession on different days. Ibn Saʿd, on the authority of ʿAtaʾ Al-Khurasani, describes them as built of palm branches with their doors covered by thick black woollen curtains. Imam Bukhari in *Al-Adab al-Mufrad*, and Baihaqi in his collection, record Dawud Ibn Qais reporting that he visited these apartments and estimated about seven cubits from the door to the roofed part of the building, the room about ten cubits, and the height of the roof about eight cubits — a cubit being about eighteen inches. These apartments of the Mothers of the Faithful were included into the Prophet's ﷺ mosque during the reign of Walid Ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, at his own command; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that on that day in Madinah people were lamenting and bewailing.

Men stand outside a curtain of black wool, close enough to be heard through it, and call for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by his bare name while he is resting.

**"Most of them have no sense."** Ibn Kathir says Allah admonished those — such as the uncivilised bedouins — who used to call to the Prophet ﷺ from behind the dwellings which belong to his wives. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this as the third etiquette in the passage: when he is at home, one should not call him from outside, and calling him by his name in particular is an unmannerly attitude — reasonable persons would not do it. That is exactly the charge: *lā yaʿqilūn*, they lack understanding. Bad adab is not merely rude here; it is a failure to grasp who is in front of you.

**Ayah 5: the cure is patience.** *"And if they had patience till you could come out to them, it would have been better for them."* Ibn Kathir notes this would have earned them the better benefit of this life and the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a fine point from the wording: *"until you come out **to them**"* is a restrictive phrase — people must wait until he emerges *to them*. If he came out for some other reason or purpose, even then it was not appropriate to press him; they should wait until a suitable occasion arises, that is, until he turns his attention to their matter.

And then the ayah ends: *"And Allah is Forgiving, Most Merciful."* After the rebuke, the open door. Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah encouraging them to turn to Him in repentance.

**Al-Aqraʿ.** Ibn Kathir notes it was reported, according to more than one source, that this ayah was revealed about Al-Aqraʿ bin Habis At-Tamimi. Imam Ahmad recorded that Al-Aqraʿ said he called the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from behind his dwellings, saying, "O Muhammad! O Muhammad!" — and according to another narration, "O Allah's Messenger!" — but the Messenger ﷺ did not answer him. Al-Aqraʿ then said, "O Allah's Messenger, my praise (of others) is worthwhile and my admonishment (of others) is degrading." The Prophet ﷺ replied: *"It is Allah the Exalted (Who is worthy of this description)."*

## Living it

This adab does not end with the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime or with his person.

**After his passing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn ʿArabi that respect for the Prophet ﷺ after his demise is just as compulsory as it was in his lifetime. On that basis some scholars expressed the view that it is disrespectful to say salām or speak very loudly in front of his blessed mausoleum; likewise, that it is discourteous to make noise where Prophetic traditions are being recited, since when his blessed words are recited it is compulsory to listen to them silently.

**Toward scholars.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some scholars ruled that the same rule applies to Islamic scholars and spiritual masters, as heirs of the Prophet ﷺ — neither proceeding ahead of them nor, as Qurtubi notes, raising voices in their assembly so loudly that their voices are suppressed. Three illustrations are given. The Prophet ﷺ saw Abu al-Darda walking in front of Abu Bakr and reprimanded him: "You are walking in front of a person who is better than you in this world and in the hereafter," adding that the sun did not rise or set on any man better than Abu Bakr in the world besides the Prophets (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from *Ruh-ul-Bayan*, on the authority of *Kashf-ul-Asrar*). Second, it is recorded in Bukhari and other collections that when Ibn ʿAbbas wished to ask a knowledgeable Companion about a Prophetic tradition, he would go to the man's house and sit at the threshold without calling him or knocking, waiting until he came out of his own accord. When the scholar said to him, "O cousin of Allah's Messenger, why did you not knock at the door and inform me of your arrival?" he replied, "A scholar in his community is like a prophet, and Allah has directed us that we should wait until he comes out on his own." Third, Abu ʿUbaidah said, "I never knock on the door of any scholar at any time; I wait until he himself has emerged, and then meet him" (*Ruh-ul-Maʿani*).

Put the passage's three commands beside one another and they describe a single disposition: **do not get ahead, do not get loud, do not get impatient.** Restrain your opinion until you know the ruling; restrain your voice where sacred words are being spoken; restrain your urgency at someone else's door. Ayah 1 makes it a matter of taqwā, ayah 3 makes it a matter of a heart tested by Allah for taqwā, and ayah 5 tells you plainly that the patient course would have been *better for them* — better, as Ibn Kathir says, in this life and in the Hereafter.

passages.title: Verifying news and the Messenger's presence
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take a single incident — a false report that almost sent an army against a Muslim tribe — and turn it into a permanent law of the believing community: verify what you are told before you act on it, and remember who among you has the better judgement. Ayah 6 gives the command to verify; ayah 7 explains why the Prophet's ﷺ view outweighed the community's in that very moment; ayah 8 credits the whole capacity for faith and right judgement to Allah alone.

## The story behind the verse

Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both anchor this passage in one event. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the account from Ibn Kathir, who reports it from the *Musnad* of Ahmad, told largely in Ḥārith's own words.

Ḥārith ibn Ḍirār ibn Abī Ḍirār was chief of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq — and father of Sayyidah Juwayriyah (may Allah be pleased with her), one of the blessed wives of the Prophet ﷺ. He came to the Prophet ﷺ, who called him to Islam and to paying Zakāh. Ḥārith accepted, and proposed a plan: he would return to his people, call them to Islam and Zakāh, and collect the alms of those who responded; on a fixed day of a fixed month the Prophet ﷺ should send a collector to receive it.

Ḥārith gathered the Zakāh. The appointed day came and went; no collector arrived. Ḥārith feared the worst — not that the Prophet ﷺ had forgotten, but that he ﷺ must be displeased with them for something. He put his worry to the leaders of his newly Muslim people and set out for Madinah.

Meanwhile the Prophet ﷺ had in fact sent a collector: Walīd ibn ʿUqbah. On the road, Walīd thought that this tribe were his old enemies, and the fear took hold of him that they meant to kill him. He turned back to Madinah and reported that they had refused to pay Zakāh and had wanted to kill him.

The Prophet ﷺ became very angry, and a force was dispatched under the command of Khālid ibn al-Walīd. An armed contingent was going out while Ḥārith with his people was coming in. They met near Madinah. "To whom have you been sent?" Ḥārith asked. "We are sent to you." "For what purpose?" They told him what Walīd had reported. Ḥārith swore: "By Allah who sent Muḥammad as His true Messenger — Walīd did not arrive in the location, nor did I see him. Since no envoy came to us at the appointed location, I feared you were annoyed with me over some shortcoming of mine. That is why I have come." Ḥārith says this verse was revealed on that occasion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then gives other versions, which it attributes to Ibn Kathir as a summary of several reports: Walīd did go to Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, and the tribe — expecting the Prophet's ﷺ envoy on the agreed date — came out of their settlement as a mark of respect to welcome him. Suspecting, on account of the old hostility, that they had come out to kill him, he turned back instantly and reported to the Prophet ﷺ, according to his suspicion, that they were unwilling to pay the alms and wanted to kill him. The Prophet ﷺ then dispatched Khālid ibn al-Walīd to make a thorough investigation so that appropriate measures could be taken. Khālid arrived near the settlement at night and encamped there, sending a few of his men in quietly to investigate; they returned reporting that the members of the tribe were Muslims and believers, regular with their prayers and in paying their alms, with nothing among them contrary to Islam. Khālid came back and reported the whole story, and on that occasion this verse was revealed.

## Ayah 6: *fa-tabayyanū* — stop and make it clear

The command is **فَتَبَيَّنُوا**, *fa-tabayyanū*: verify it, make sure of it. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah's order to investigate the news that sinners and the wicked bring and make sure of its authenticity. His reasoning is sharp: if a sinner's word is taken for granted and a decision is based on it — whether the information is true or not — then the authorities are effectively taking the lead *of* the sinners, and Allah has forbidden taking the path of the corrupted and the sinners. Ibn Kathir draws a striking consequence: this is why groups of the scholars of Hadith refuse to accept narrations from narrators whose reliability is unknown, since such a narrator might in reality be among the wicked people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes another reading of the word, *tathabbatū*, carrying the same meaning: **be steady**. Do not rush into taking actions or measures; be stable and stand firmly in your place, and do not be easily moved or shaken; wait until the news is confirmed by other independent sources.

Then note *why*: **أَن تُصِيبُوا قَوْمًا بِجَهَالَةٍ** — "lest you harm a people out of ignorance, and afterwards you become regretful for what you have done." The danger is not merely being wrong; it is *striking* people while ignorant, and then living with the regret. Nothing you do afterwards un-strikes them.

## What the jurists built on this ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ruling plainly: if a mischief-monger, sinner, wicked or corrupt person complains about any person or nation, or accuses them of any wrongdoing, it is not lawful to act upon the sole information or evidence of such a person without making a thorough investigation.

Imam Jaṣṣāṣ, in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān*, presses further. Since it is not lawful to accept and act on a sinful person's report until it is investigated and confirmed from other sources, the **testimony** of such a person would be unacceptable with even greater force — because every testimony is a statement confirmed by a kind of oath. Hence, according to the majority of scholars, the statement or evidence of an ungodly person is, in Sharīʿah terms, not acceptable.

But — and this keeps a mercy from becoming a burden — **all scholars agree** that as far as common worldly affairs are concerned, it is not necessary to ascertain the accuracy of every item of news and the reliability of every informant. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: the rule is governed by an effective cause laid down in the explicit text of the verse itself — *lest you harm a people out of ignorance* (49:6) — so matters not governed by that cause are an exception to it. The example given: if a wicked person, or for that matter even an unbeliever, delivers a gift saying it was sent by a certain person, it is lawful to accept both the gift and the statement. The ayah is no licence for corrosive suspicion of everyone you meet; it bites precisely where acting on a report could **injure** someone.

## "Was a Companion called a *fāsiq*?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the difficulty honestly. Authentic aḥādīth verify that this verse was revealed in connection with Walīd ibn ʿUqbah, and the verse speaks of a *fāsiq* (a sinner, an ungodly person). Apparently, then, a Companion could be a *fāsiq* — which conflicts with the universally established maxim that the Companions are all truthful and reliable. Two answers are given, worth keeping distinct.

**First, ʿAllāmah Ālūsī's answer in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*.** According to the majority of scholars the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) are not infallible: it is possible for them to commit sins, including major sins, which is *fisq*; at such a time they are dealt with in the appropriate manner in terms of the punishment prescribed for that act, and if any were found guilty of lying, his report or testimony would be rejected. Yet on the basis of the express texts of the Qurʼān and Sunnah, Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jamāʿah hold that although a Companion may commit a sin, they do not persist in it — there is none who did not repent and purify himself after a sin. Of the general class of the Companions the Qurʼān announces in general terms: **رَّضِيَ اللَّـهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ** — "Allah is well-pleased with them and they are well-pleased with Him" (98:8) — and the pleasure of Allah is not possible without forgiveness of sins.

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā, quoted from Ibn Taymiyyah in *al-Ṣārim al-Maslūl*: Allah's pleasure is one of His eternal attributes, and He expresses His pleasure only for those about whom He knows they will die while seeking His pleasure.

So: from that magnificent group it was possible for a handful to commit a sin at some point, but divine aid came to their rescue and they repented immediately. Through the blessing of the Prophet's ﷺ company Allah had made the Sharīʿah their nature, so it was very rare for them to do anything contrary to it. In comparison to the uncountable good works and merits to their credit, even a single sin in a lifetime would be quashed or counted as non-existent — **إِنَّ الْحَسَنَاتِ يُذْهِبْنَ السَّيِّئَاتِ**, "Surely, good deeds erase bad deeds" (Sūrah Hūd 114) — and this applies to them with greater force, since their good deeds are not like the good deeds of the general class of people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the collections of Abū Dāwūd and Tirmidhī, on the authority of Saʿīd ibn Zayd: "By Allah, anyone of them who participated in a jihad with the Holy Prophet ﷺ and his face got covered with dust is better than your life-long obedience and worship, even if you attained the age of Nūḥ (peace be upon him)." Hence: they receive whatever penalty is prescribed for an act they may have committed, but it is not lawful for any of us to regard any of them as a *fāsiq*. A momentary lapse never becomes a permanent characteristic or title.

**Second, and more directly**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that it is not at all necessary that the verse refers to Walīd ibn ʿUqbah as a *fāsiq*. That it was revealed over his incident does not mean the word is used for him; before this he had done nothing on account of which he could be so called. An analysis of the incident shows that what he conveyed was **incorrect information which, acting in good faith, he thought was true** while in reality it was not. So the plain import of the ayah is a general rule — the news conveyed by a *fāsiq* is unacceptable — while Walīd's information was not acted upon because strong external context made it seem unacceptable, which is why the Prophet ﷺ refrained from taking measures merely on his report and sent Khālid for proper investigation. Hence the argument from the stronger case: if that is how the news of a bona fide reliable and righteous person is handled, a *fāsiq*'s news deserves rejection all the more.

## Ayah 7: "And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah"

**وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ فِيكُمْ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ.** Ibn Kathir unfolds it: know that among you is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — therefore honour and respect him, be polite with him, and obey his orders, for he is more knowledgeable about what benefits you and is more concerned with you than you yourselves are, and his opinions in such matters are more complete than your own. He brings the parallel **النَّبِيُّ أَوْلَىٰ بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْ أَنْفُسِهِمْ** — "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves" (33:6).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties this back to the story, citing Mazharī. When Walīd's report arrived, the blessed Companions were disturbed and infuriated, and expressed the view that jihād should be declared immediately; the Prophet ﷺ rejected the report on the basis of strong circumstantial evidence to the contrary and sent Khālid to investigate. So ayah 6 gave a rule about doubtful reports; ayah 7 adds one more guideline. In substance: your reaction came out of religious zeal and enthusiasm — yet your view was not right and proper, and the decision taken by the Prophet ﷺ proved to be better.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the etiquette of consultation: in matters requiring consultation it is proper to express a view, but not proper to exert efforts to get the Prophet ﷺ to act upon your opinion. There is a rare possibility that an opinion he ﷺ expresses on some worldly matter comes to be against worldly expedience — and this is not contrary to the station of his prophethood — yet Allah gifted him with insight, perspicacity and discernment which you do not have. Even where your opinion is rarely right and proper, it is still better to abandon it and obey him ﷺ: whatever worldly loss you suffer that way would not be as harmful as his following your opinion, and the reward of obedience is a better compensation.

**لَوْ يُطِيعُكُمْ فِي كَثِيرٍ مِنَ الْأَمْرِ لَعَنِتُّمْ** — "If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would surely be in trouble." Ibn Kathir: if he obeys all of your opinions and desires, you will earn trouble and hardship. This is Allah clarifying that they fall short in overseeing their own benefit; Ibn Kathir cites **وَلَوِ اتَّبَعَ الْحَقُّ أَهْوَاءَهُمْ لَفَسَدَتِ السَّمَاوَاتُ وَالْأَرْضُ وَمَن فِيهِنَّ** — "And if the truth had been in accordance with their desires, verily the heavens and the earth and whosoever is therein would have been corrupted" (23:71).

The word *laʿanittum* rewards a pause. Qurṭubī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, notes that lexically it connotes both "to commit a sin or crime" and "to suffer from hardship" — and in this context both connotations appropriately fit. Had the Prophet ﷺ moved as the community wished, they would have fallen into wrongdoing *and* into hardship in one stroke.

## "But Allah endeared faith to you"

**وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ حَبَّبَ إِلَيْكُمُ الْإِيمَانَ وَزَيَّنَهُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ** — "But Allah has endeared the faith to you and has beautified it in your hearts." Ibn Kathir: He made faith dear to your souls and beautified it in your hearts. The very zeal that made them want to march was itself, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it, religious zeal and enthusiasm — faith made dear to them, so that a report of apostasy stung.

**وَكَرَّهَ إِلَيْكُمُ الْكُفْرَ وَالْفُسُوقَ وَالْعِصْيَانَ** — "and has made disbelief, *fusūq* and *ʿiṣyān* hateful to you." Ibn Kathir glosses the three: disbelief; sins, whether major or minor; and *ʿiṣyān*, all types of sins. This statement, he observes, "transfers us from one level to a better level, to perfect Allah's bounty" — it is not only that falsehood is kept from you, but that your heart is retuned to find it repellent. And **أُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الرَّاشِدُونَ** — those who have these qualities, says Ibn Kathir, are the rightly guided ones whom Allah has granted guidance and correctness.

## The Prophet ﷺ asked for exactly this

Ibn Kathir records here that Imam Ahmad reported from Abū Rifāʿah al-Zuraqī, from his father: during the battle of Uḥud, when the idolaters retreated, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Stay in straight lines so that I praise my Lord, the Exalted and Most Honoured." They stood behind him in lines, and he ﷺ made a long supplication — that Allah's is all the praise; that there is none who can withhold what He sends or send what He withholds, guide whom He sends astray or misguide whom He guides — and, within it:

> "O Allah! Make faith dear to us and beautify it in our hearts, and make disbelief, *fusūq* and *ʿiṣyān* hateful to us, and make us among the rightly guided."

Those are the words of ayah 7, turned into a request. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Nasāʼī collected this hadith in *ʿAmal al-Yawm wal-Laylah*. What Allah announces as a favour already granted, the Prophet ﷺ still asked for — because a heart that loves faith today needs Allah to keep it loving faith tomorrow.

## Ayah 8: whose achievement is it?

**فَضْلًا مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَنِعْمَةً** — "a grace from Allah and His favour." Ibn Kathir: this favour that He has bestowed on you is a favour and a bounty from Him to you. Everything just described — faith made dear, sin made repellent, right guidance — is credited back to the Giver. You did not manufacture your own love of īmān.

**وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ** — "And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise." Ibn Kathir: All-Knower of those who deserve guidance and those who deserve misguidance; All-Wise in His statements, actions, legislation, and the destiny He appoints. The names land with force here: the whole crisis came of people acting on incomplete knowledge, and the passage closes by naming the One whose knowledge is never so.

## Living it

**Check before you strike.** The test is not "is this interesting?" but "could acting on this injure someone?" Where it could, the report needs independent confirmation first; where it could not — the jurists' own example of a gift delivered with a message — the rule does not apply. Note too the subtler lesson in Walīd's case: fear, old hostility, and suspicion delivered as fact are enough; you do not need a liar to get a catastrophe.

**Hold your opinion with an open hand.** Express your view where consultation calls for it; do not exert yourself to have that view prevail over the Prophet's ﷺ guidance. Religious zeal is real and good — the Companions' anger came from exactly that — and it is still not the same thing as being right. And ask, as he ﷺ asked at Uḥud: *O Allah, make faith dear to us, beautify it in our hearts, and make us among the rightly guided.*

passages.title: Reconciling believers who fight each other
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat take the hardest case in a community's life — believers with weapons in their hands, fighting one another — and refuse to let it dissolve the bond of faith. Ayah 10 gives the reason underneath the procedure of ayah 9: **the believers are but a brotherhood** — so what looks like crisis management is really the repair of a family.

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the link with what precedes. The earlier ayat set out the rights of the Prophet ﷺ and the manner in which he is to be treated, prohibiting any act that would annoy or hurt him. This set of ayat, 9–10, then establishes the manners, mores, injunctions, and mutual rights and obligations to be observed in individual and social life. The common value running through all of these rules, Maʿārif notes, is **to avoid causing any inconvenience to the members of the society**. Ayat 9–10 are that principle applied at its breaking point.

## What actually happened

Ibn Kathir preserves two accounts of the occasion of revelation, and both are strikingly small-scale.

Saʿid bin Jubayr said that the tribes of **Aws and Khazraj** once got into a scuffle using date-tree branches and slippers, and Allah revealed this honourable ayah commanding that peace be made between them.

As-Suddi gives a fuller story. A man of the Ansar named ʿImran had a wife called Umm Zayd. She wanted to visit her family; he prevented her by locking her in an upper room, so none of her family could visit or even see her. She sent word to them. They came, brought her down from the room, and wanted to take her away — her husband being absent at the time. His family called on their people; their cousins came to prevent the wife going with her family. A push-and-shove situation turned into a fight using slippers. This ayah was revealed in their case, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent someone to bring peace between them, and both sides agreed to resort to the decision of Allah the Exalted.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful note. Commentators narrate several incidents as the background here, among them a clash between two Muslim groups; it is not inconceivable that the totality of them was the occasion of revelation, or that one was the actual cause and the others, being similar, came to be called occasions of revelation too.

## "Two groups of the believers"

Ibn Kathir writes: **Allah calls both opposing groups among the Muslims "believers", although they are fighting each other.**

He then reports that al-Bukhari and other scholars relied on this as evidence that **committing a sin does not nullify faith, no matter how major the sin is** — a creed that contradicts the creed of the Khawarij, and of those who accepted their idea, such as the Muʿtazilah. Sin wounds faith; it does not automatically cancel it.

## The procedure of ayah 9

**First: reconcile.** *Fa-aṣliḥū baynahumā* — "then make peace between them both." Ibn Kathir opens with the plain command: Allah commands making peace between Muslims that fight each other. Not the two fighting parties are addressed, but everyone else. Reconciliation is the standing obligation of the bystanders.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the immediate addressees are rulers and those in authority, who have the means to fight and wage war — this is stated by Abu Hayyan in *Al-Baḥr* and preferred by Alusi in *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī* — while all Muslims are addressed indirectly, to assist those in authority in this matter. And where there is no leader, amīr, king or president? Then, from *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*: the two warring parties are to be advised, as far as possible, to cease war; and if that is not possible, common people are ordered to **stay away from both warring groups — neither opposing nor aiding either one**.

**Second: restrain the transgressor.** *Fa-in baghat iḥdāhumā ʿalā'l-ukhrā* — if one of them outrages against the other, then fight the one that outrages "till it complies with the command of Allah." Ibn Kathir explains: **until the rebellious group refers to the commands of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ for judgement, and they listen to and obey the truth.** The goal is never the defeat of the group; it is their return to the ruling of Allah.

Ibn Kathir brings the Prophet's ﷺ teaching that makes sense of this. In a hadith in the Ṣaḥiḥ, Anas states that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or he is oppressed."* Anas asked: it is right that I help him if he is oppressed, but how should I help him if he is an oppressor? He ﷺ said, *"By preventing him from oppressing others; this is how you help him in this case."*

Restraining the aggressor is not the opposite of brotherhood — it *is* brotherhood, performed on the man who is wronging himself by wronging others.

**Third: settle it with justice.** *Fa-in fāʼat fa-aṣliḥū baynahumā bi'l-ʿadl wa aqsiṭū* — "then if it complies, make reconciliation between them justly, and be equitable." The verb *fāʼat* is rendered by Maʿārif as "comes back": the picture is of return, not of humiliation.

Ibn Kathir glosses the command simply — **be fair in your judgement regarding the dispute that occurred between them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something deeper: if the belligerent party ceases fighting, do not only stop the fighting, but **think about eliminating the cause of war and mutual dissatisfaction, so that the heart-burnings may come to an end** — so that an atmosphere of brotherhood may prevail for all times to come. And why the heavy stress on equity? Because, Maʿārif notes, these people had fought against the Muslim ruler, and it was possible that he would not treat them equitably afterwards. So the Qur'an lays stress on setting things right between them equitably and justly, so that the rights of no one are violated. (Adapted from *Bayān ul-Qurʼān* with reference to *Hidāyah*.)

Then the seal: *inna'llāha yuḥibbu'l-muqsiṭīn* — "Verily, Allah loves those who are the equitable." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Verily, those who are equitable in this life will be on podiums made of pearls before Ar-Raḥmān, the Exalted and Most Honoured, on account of their fairness in this life."* An-Nasaʼi collected this hadith.

## The rulings that follow

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the jurists' framework. There are several forms of mutual fighting between two Muslim parties: both are subjects of a Muslim government; neither is; or one is and the other is not.

In the first case it is **compulsory on common Muslims** to bring about an understanding between them and try to stop the mutual fighting. If they do not cease fighting by negotiations, it becomes imperative for the Muslim ruler to take measures against them. If both parties then cease through the intervention of the Islamic government, the laws of retaliation, retribution and blood-wit apply. If they do not cease, both are treated like rebels. If one withdraws and the other persists in oppression and transgression, the persistent group is treated like a rebel group, and the obedient one is designated *ʿādil* — just.

The law of rebels itself is notably restrained. Before fighting, their weapons must be seized and confiscated. They are then arrested and kept in prison until they repent. **Neither during the fighting nor after it are their children to be enslaved**. **Their wealth is not treated like the spoils of war** — it is held in trust until they repent, and after repentance their belongings are returned to them. This is not the law of war against an enemy; it is the discipline of a family member who has to be restrained and then received back.

**Hearing the grievance first.** Maʿārif states the ruling plainly: if a very powerful group of Muslims revolts against the Muslim ruler, it is necessary for the ruler **first to hear out their complaint** or the cause of their dissatisfaction. If a doubt or misunderstanding has arisen in their minds about some matter, it should be removed. If they show such cause on the basis of which it is permissible in the Sharīʿah to oppose a Muslim leader or ruler — such as unjust behaviour on the part of the government — then it is essential for the general body of Muslims **to assist that group**, so that the ruler may refrain from his tyranny, *provided that his tyranny is proved beyond any shadow of doubt* (Ibn ul-Humām; Mazharī). If they cannot show any clearly legitimate reason for their dissatisfaction, revolt and war against the Muslim ruler, then it is permitted to wage war against the rebels.

**Imam ash-Shafiʿi (raḥimahullāh) held that the Muslims should not initiate fighting against the rebels unless the rebels first start the fight** (Mazharī).

**When you cannot tell who is right.** All of the above applies when it is positively and unquestionably clear that a group is rebellious. But if it is difficult to determine which group is rebellious and which is just — because each party has a valid Sharīʿah argument to justify its course of action — then the pros and cons of both are weighed to determine the "just" party on the principle of probability. If one party's juristic argument seems more convincing to a person, it is permitted for him to assist that group. **If he cannot prefer the standpoint of either, he should remain neutral** — as happened in the civil wars of the Battle of the Camel and the Battle of Ṣiffīn, when many noble Companions ؓ remained aloof.

## The Companions ؓ, and how we speak of them

Ibn Kathir sets a Prophetic word over this whole history. Al-Bukhari narrated that al-Hasan said that Abu Bakrah said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a speech on the minbar while al-Hasan bin ʿAli was with him. He was repeatedly looking at al-Hasan and then at the people; then he said, *"Verily, this son of mine is a sayyid (a chief or master), and may Allah make peace between two great groups of Muslims through him."* What the Prophet ﷺ said occurred: al-Hasan brought peace between the people of ash-Sham and ʿIraq, after they fought tremendous wars and frightening battles.

Imam Abu Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabi says that this ayah about battle between Muslims **covers all cases**, including where both parties prepare for war on the grounds of a principle of the Sharīʿah — and the civil wars of the noble Companions ؓ were of this nature. Qurtubi quotes this view, explains the actual situation of the Battle of the Camel and the Battle of Ṣiffīn, and draws guidelines for later generations. Maʿārif summarises the position, with reference to Qurtubi:

It is **not permitted to attribute categorically, and with certainty, to any of the Companions that he was absolutely wrong** in his action, because each of them acted according to his own *ijtihād* — his sincere exertion to reach the correct ruling — and their objective was to seek the pleasure of Allah. The Companions ؓ are all our leaders; it is enjoined upon us that we hold back our tongues from talking about their mutual differences and always speak the best things about them. The Prophet's companionship is a highly honourable position which must not be violated. The Prophet ﷺ prohibited reviling them or talking badly about them, and informed us that they have been forgiven and that Allah is pleased with them.

Maʿārif then reasons from the reports. There is the hadith regarding Sayyidna Ṭalḥah ؓ, reaching us through several transmitting authorities: *"Ṭalḥah is a martyr walking on the face of the earth."* Had Ṭalḥah ؓ been committing a clear sin by going out to wage war against Sayyidna ʿAli ؓ, he could not have attained the high status of a martyr — for **martyrdom is attained only when a person is killed in obedience to Allah**. Similarly, Sayyidna ʿAli ؓ himself reports that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The killer of Zubayr is in Hell," and that he ﷺ said, "Give news to the killer of Sayyidah Ṣafiyyah's ؓ son that he will be in Hell." In the light of this, Maʿārif concludes, we need to believe that **Sayyidna Zubayr and Sayyidna Ṭalḥah ؓ were not sinners nor disobedient to Allah in the position they took in the battle**. Maʿārif notes that traditions relating to this subject have almost reached the grade of continuity (*tawātur*) — that is, transmission by so many independent chains that the report is beyond reasonable doubt.

Those Companions ؓ who took part on neither side are likewise not to be regarded as defaulters: their conduct in the matter was also based on their *ijtihād*. It is not proper in any sense of the word to curse them, taunt them, hold them as sinners, or neglect their virtues, their struggles and their great religious stations.

Maʿārif closes with the voices of the early scholars:

- Asked about the blood shed in those battles, some scholars simply recited: *"Those are a people who have passed away. For them what they earned, and for you what you earned. And you shall not be questioned as to what they have been doing"* (2:134).
- Another, asked the same, replied: **"Allah saved my hands from being soiled with that blood. Now I will not soil my tongue with it."** He meant that he did not wish to make the mistake of categorically adjudging any one of the groups the defaulter.
- ʿAllāmah Ibn Fūrak (raḥimahullāh) relates that some of his colleagues felt the conflicts between the noble Companions ؓ were like the episodes of conflict between Sayyidna Yusuf (ʿalayhi's-salām) and his brothers: despite their mutual differences they did not lose their status of *wilāyah* (nearness to Allah, being among His close friends) and *nubuwwah* (prophethood). The same principle, they held, applies here.
- Sayyidna Muḥāsibi (raḥimahullāh): "As far as this bloodshed is concerned, it is difficult for us to say anything, because there was a difference of opinion in this regard among the noble Companions ؓ themselves."
- Hasan al-Basri (raḥimahullāh), when asked: **"Those were fights in which the Companions were present and we were not. They knew all the circumstances and we do not know them. The matter in which the Companions are unanimous, we follow; and the matter in which there is difference of opinion, we observe silence."** Sayyidna Muḥāsibi (raḥimahullāh) said: we concur with Hasan al-Basri.

## Ayah 10: the reason under the ruling

*Innama'l-muʼminūna ikhwah* — "The believers are but a brotherhood." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line: **all of them are brothers in Islam.** The wording is restrictive — they *are but* a brotherhood. This is what believers are, not what they become when they get along.

Ibn Kathir gathers the Prophet's ﷺ words on what that brotherhood costs and gives:

- *"The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim; he is not unjust with him nor does he forsake him."*
- In the Ṣaḥiḥ: *"Allah helps the servant as long as the servant helps his brother."*
- Also in the Ṣaḥiḥ: *"If the Muslim invokes Allah for the benefit of his absent brother, the angel says afterwards: Āmīn, and for you the same."*
- In the Ṣaḥiḥ: *"The parable of the believers in relation to the kindness, mercy and compassion they have for each other is that of the body: when an organ of it falls ill, the rest of the body responds with fever and sleeplessness."*
- And also in the Ṣaḥiḥ: *"A believer to another believer is like a building whose different parts reinforce each other"* — and the Prophet ﷺ then clasped his hands with the fingers interlaced.

Then: *fa-aṣliḥū bayna akhawaykum*, "so make reconciliation between your brothers." Ibn Kathir says this refers back to **the two groups that fight each other**. The shift of word is the whole argument of the passage in miniature: in ayah 9 they were two *ṭāʼifah*, two parties at war; in ayah 10 they are your two *brothers*. Same people, seen from Allah's angle.

The passage ends with *wa'ttaqū'llāha laʿallakum turḥamūn*. Ibn Kathir: have taqwā of Allah — mindful fear of Him that keeps you from His displeasure — **in all of your affairs**; and "that you may receive mercy" is **a promise from Allah that He will grant mercy to those who fear and obey Him**.

## Living it

- **Reconciliation is a duty of the uninvolved.** The command in both ayat is addressed to those who are not fighting. Standing back and calling it "not my business" is not neutrality; it is neglect of an order.
- **Take the small fight seriously** — revelation came down over a scuffle with palm branches and slippers.
- **Do not let a quarrel redefine the person.** Allah kept calling them believers mid-battle; ayah 10 calls them your brothers.
- **Helping a wrongdoer means stopping him** — the Prophet's ﷺ answer to Anas. Loyalty that lets a friend continue in oppression is not loyalty.
- **Peace-making is not finished when the fighting stops.** Maʿārif: remove the cause, so the heart-burning ends.
- **Be equitable even toward the side that was in the wrong** — that is exactly where the temptation to unfairness lies, and exactly where Allah says He loves those who are equitable.
- **Where the truth is genuinely unclear, silence and neutrality are legitimate** — the counsel of Hasan al-Basri, and the practice of Companions ؓ who remained aloof from both sides.

passages.title: Mockery, suspicion, backbiting, and true honour
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form one argument. Ayat 11 and 12 name six ways a believer wounds another believer — mockery, fault-finding, insulting nicknames, unfounded suspicion, spying, backbiting — and ayah 13 pulls the ground out from under all six: every human being descends from one man and one woman, and the only real rank is taqwā.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the surah's movement: its opening verses laid down the Prophet's ﷺ rights and the manners due to him; now the Qur'an turns to the manners owed between individuals.

## Ayah 11: mockery, fault-finding, nicknames

**Mockery.** Ibn Kathir explains that scoffing at people "implies humiliating and belittling them." Qurtubi, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, widens the net: mocking includes mimicking someone, making pointed references to him, laughing at his words, his works, his appearance or his dress. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith recorded *in the Sahih* in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"Arrogance is refusing the truth and belittling people"** — another version has **"and despising people."** Mockery is arrogance wearing a joke as a disguise.

**"It may be that they are better than them."** The reason the Qur'an gives is devastating because it is uncertain. You do not know. Ibn Kathir writes that the injured party "could be more honored and dearer to Allah the Exalted than those who ridicule and belittle them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it bluntly: no one may mock a person whose body or face is defective, impaired or deformed, because he does not know that in Allah's sight that person may be the better of the two, on account of his sincerity and purity of heart.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, has the Prophet ﷺ saying: **"Allah does not look at your Faces and your wealth; He looks at your hearts and your works."** Qurtubi derives a legal maxim: it is not proper to pass a categorical judgment on the basis of overt evidence or circumstances. Outward actions may seem good yet be bad in Allah's sight because of an insincere heart; they may seem bad yet, because of a pure heart, serve as an expiation of bad actions.

**"Nor defame yourselves" (walā talmizū anfusakum).** Ibn Kathir explains the pair of sins named in 104:1, "Woe to every *Humazah*, *Lumazah*": *hamz* is defamation by action, *lamz* by words. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Qatādah and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān all read "yourselves" as "none of you should defame each other." Both commentaries compare 4:29, "Nor kill yourselves," which means "nor kill one another." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic: a Muslim is the brother of another Muslim, so killing one's brother is like killing oneself. In the same way, when you find fault with others and upbraid them, others will find fault with you, "because no man is normally free from any fault." Hence the scholars' maxim: *"You have faults and people have eyes."*

**Nicknames — and why this ayah came down.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Jābirah ibn aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "This Ayah was revealed about us, Banū Salamah. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Al-Madinah, every man among us had two or three nicknames. When the Prophet ﷺ called a man by one of these nicknames, people would say, 'O Allah's Messenger! He hates that nickname.' Then this Ayah was revealed." Abu Dawud also collected this hadith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some of those names had been popularised in order to denigrate their bearer; the Prophet ﷺ was not aware of this, and sometimes used them unwittingly, until the Companions informed him.

So the prohibition means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "you should not address people by nick names that people dislike." Ibn ʿAbbās extends it: if a person committed a sin from which he repented and mended his ways, it is unlawful for anyone to call him by denigrating names such as thief, adulterer or drunkard. Qurtubi cites a report that the Prophet ﷺ said that anyone who denigrates a Muslim for a sin of which he has repented, Allah takes it upon Himself that He will get that person to commit the very same sin and expose him to humiliation in this world and in the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, from Qurtubi, that titles which sound offensive but serve only to identify are permitted — which is why the scholars of hadith allowed epithets like *al-Aʿraj* (the lame) or *al-Aḥdab* (the hunchbacked) in the chains of transmission, provided no insult is meant. The positive duty runs the other way too: it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that a believer has a right to be called by the good names he likes best — which is why he ﷺ gave ʿUmar the title *al-Fārūq* and Ḥamzah the title *Asadullāh*.

**"Evil is the name of wickedness after faith."** Ibn Kathir reads this as: to use the nicknames used by the people of *Jāhiliyyah* after you embraced Islam and understood it. Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani turns the ayah round: the real bad name for a person after embracing faith is that he is known among people for sinful acts. So if a Muslim commits the sin of calling others bad nicknames and becomes known for it, *he* has earned the bad name. And whoever does not repent of this sin, Allah names among the wrongdoers.

## Ayah 12: suspicion, spying, backbiting

The three sins here run in sequence: a thought, an investigation, a broadcast.

**Suspicion (ẓann).** Notice the precision — "avoid *much* suspicion, indeed *some* suspicion is sin." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that not all types of suspicion are a sin, so it is incumbent on us to investigate which type is. *Ẓann* primarily denotes an assumption on probable evidence; Qurtubi says it carries here the sense of *accusation* — a charge of wrongdoing, guilt or blame without any strong evidence.

Imam Abu Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ, in *Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*, sorts ẓann into four categories. **Prohibited**: distrust of Allah — thinking that He will punish him or keep him in calamity forever, thus despairing of His grace — and entertaining suspicion without rational grounds about Muslims whose outward conditions show them to be good. Jābir reports the Prophet ﷺ saying, "None of you should die without having favourable thoughts about Allah," and according to another hadith Allah says, **"I treat my servants the way they think about me."** **Imperative**: where a decision must be made and there is no clear-cut proof from Qur'an and Sunnah for that situation, one must act on *al-ẓann al-ghālib*, the best possible assessment. **Permissible**: a worshipper unsure whether he has performed three rakʿāt or four, who may complete the prayer on best assessment. **Desirable**: having favourable thoughts about every Muslim.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "Never think ill of the word that comes out of your believing brother's mouth, as long as you can find a good excuse for it."

Malik recorded that Abu Hurayrah reported the Prophet ﷺ saying: **"Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the worst of false tales; do not spy on one another; do not look for other's faults; do not be jealous of one another; do not envy one another; do not hate one another; and do not desert (shun) one another. And O Allah's servants! Be brothers!"** The Two Sahihs and Abu Dawud recorded this hadith as well.

**Spying (tajassus).** Ibn Kathir notes that *tajassus* usually harbours ill intentions — the spy is called a *jāsūs* — while *taḥassus* (inquiring) is usually done for a good reason, as in Yaʿqūb's words, "O my sons! Go you and inquire about Yusuf and his brother" (12:87); yet both terms could have evil connotations, and in the Sahih the Prophet ﷺ forbade both.

The rule, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: one may take into account what is presented in evidence, but it is not permitted to search for faults that are not overt. It cites, via Qurtubi, the Prophet's ﷺ words: "Do not speak ill of Muslims behind their backs, and do not search out their faults, for he who searches out their faults will have his faults searched out by Allah, and he whose faults are searched out by Allah will be exposed by Him, even though he should be in the interior of his house." *Bayān al-Qurʾān* records one exception: where there is apprehension that mischief-makers may harm the community, it is permitted to investigate them.

**Backbiting (ghībah).** Abu Dawud collected that Abu Hurayrah said: "It was asked, 'O Allah's Messenger! What is backbiting?' He ﷺ said, **'Mentioning about your brother in a manner that he dislikes.'** He was asked, 'What if my brother was as I mentioned?' He ﷺ said, **'If he was as you mentioned, you will have committed backbiting. But if he was not as you say about him, you will have falsely accused him.'"** At-Tirmidhi collected it and said *"Hasan Sahih."* Truth is no defence — and if it is false, it is slander, heavier still.

**The image.** "Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would hate it." Ibn Kathir's comment is exact: just as you hate eating the flesh of a dead person *on account of your nature*, so hate backbiting *on account of your religion* — and the latter carries a punishment that is worse than the former. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completes the picture: if the victim is present, disgracing him is like eating the flesh of a living person, which ayah 11 calls *lamz*; if he is absent, it is like eating the flesh of a dead one.

Why is backbiting condemned most severely? Because a man insulted to his face can defend himself; whereas the absent man has no one to defend him. Hence the duty: defend your brother when people speak ill of him in his absence, and if that is not possible, at least abstain from listening — because listening to it wilfully is like backbiting itself.

**The warnings.** Ibn Kathir cites, through various chains of narration in the Sahihs and Musnads, the Prophet's ﷺ words during the Farewell Hajj: **"Verily, your blood, wealth and honor are as sacred among you as the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this town of yours."**

Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abu Yaʿlā recorded — with what Ibn Kathir calls an authentic chain of narration — that after Māʿiz was stoned for adultery, the Prophet ﷺ heard two men saying to one another, "Have you not seen the man who had Allah cover his secret, but his heart could not let him rest until he was stoned to death, just as the dog is stoned?" Passing the corpse of a donkey, he ﷺ said, **"Where are so-and-so? Dismount and eat from this donkey."** They said, "May Allah forgive you, O Allah's Messenger! Would anyone eat this meat?" He replied: **"The backbiting you committed against your brother is worse as a meal than this meal. By He in Whose Hand is my soul! He is now swimming in the rivers of Paradise."** And from Abu Saʿīd and Jābir, transmitted by Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud as cited in Mazhari: "Backbiting is worse than adultery." He ﷺ replied: "A person may commit fornication, repent of it and his sin is forgiven. But the sin of backbiting is not forgiven unless the injured party forgives."

**Repenting from it.** The ayah closes with mercy: "And have Taqwa of Allah. Verily, Allah is the One Who forgives and accepts repentance, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir reports that the majority of scholars hold that repentance from backbiting is to refrain from it, intending not to repeat it; and he records disagreement over whether remorse is required, and whether one must apologise to the person backbitten. Some scholars said it is not necessary to ask them for forgiveness; better, they said, to praise those you backbit in the very gatherings where you disparaged them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the same split — the hadith above makes backbiting a violation of a human right requiring the victim's pardon, while other scholars (an-Nawawī, Ibn aṣ-Ṣalāḥ and others quoted in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*) held that it does not become a human right unless the injured party comes to know of it, so seeking his pardon is not necessary. Where the victim has died or disappeared, a narration of Anas transmitted by Bayhaqī and cited in Mazhari gives the atonement — to invoke Allah's forgiveness for him: **"O Allah, forgive our sins and his sins."**

**Where mentioning a person's faults is allowed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists needs the Sharīʿah recognises as genuine: complaining against a tyrant before someone who can relieve the injustice; giving a full account of a case in order to obtain a fatwa; warning Muslims of a mischief-monger; apprising someone who consults you of all aspects; and mentioning the bad deeds of one who sins openly and publicises his own ungodly behaviour. The necessary condition throughout is that speaking ill is not intended to insult or disgrace, but only to fulfil a genuine need.

## Ayah 13: the ground beneath it all

**The address changes.** Ayat 11 and 12 begin "O you who believe." Ayah 13 begins **"O mankind"** — the argument widens to the human race. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah created them all from a single person, Adam, and from that person He created his mate, Ḥawwāʾ. "Therefore, all people are the descendants of Adam and Ḥawwāʾ and share this honor equally. The only difference between them is in the religion that revolves around their obedience to Allah the Exalted and their following of His Messenger ﷺ."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle: the verse lays the axe to false notions of superiority born of racial arrogance or national conceit. No one may take pride, nor degrade others, on the basis of the pigment of his skin, the amount of wealth he possesses, descent or pedigree — but only by his moral uprightness and the way he discharges his obligations to Allah and to man. The entire human race is but one family.

**The occasion of revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that this verse was revealed at the conquest of Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ asked Bilāl to call the adhān. Ḥārith ibn Hishām remarked, "Could Muhammad not find anyone better than this black crow to sound the adhān in the Sacred Mosque!" Jibrīl came down and told the Prophet ﷺ of the conversation; he called them, and they admitted it. At this, the verse was revealed. On the report of Baghawī cited in Mazhari, the Prophet ﷺ told them: "You are empty" — you have no moral leg to stand on — "Bilāl, on the other hand, is equipped; and he is better and more honourable than any of you."

**"That you may know one another" (li-taʿārafū).** Recognition, not ranking, is the stated purpose of human difference. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *shuʿūb* as the plural of *shaʿb*, a large group of persons of the same origin, like a nation — the largest grouping, subdividing down to the *ʿashīrah*, the smallest. Mujāhid glossed *li-taʿārafū* as one's saying, "So-and-so the son of so-and-so, from the tribe of so-and-so." Lineage serves real purposes — distinguishing two people who bear the same name, discharging Sharʿī rights, determining heirs — so referring to one's lineage for identification is not deemed pride and conceit.

**"Verily, the most honorable of you with Allah is the one who has At-Taqwa."** Ibn Kathir: you earn honour with Allah on account of taqwā, not family lineage. Al-Bukhari narrated that Abu Hurayrah said some people asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Who is the most honorable among people?" He replied, **"The most honorable among them with Allah is the one who has the most Taqwa."** They said, "We did not ask you about this." He said, **"Then the most honorable person is Yusuf, Allah's Prophet, the son of Allah's Prophet, the son of Allah's Prophet, the son of Allah's Khalil."** They said again that this was not their question — they meant Arab lineage. He said, **"Those among you who were best in Jahiliyyah, are the best among you in Islam, if they attain religious understanding."** Lineage is not erased, only demoted beneath taqwā and understanding of the religion.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar that on the day Makkah was conquered the Prophet ﷺ made ṭawāf riding his camel al-Qaṣwāʾ, then gave a sermon from her back: **"O people! Allah the Exalted has removed from you the slogans of Jahiliyyah and its tradition of honoring forefathers. Men are of two types, a man who is righteous, fearful of Allah and honorable to Allah, or a man who is vicious, miserable and little to Allah the Exalted."** Then he recited this very ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits the same sermon from Tirmidhi and Baghawī.

**"Verily, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware" (ʿAlīm, Khabīr).** Ibn Kathir: He is All-Knowing of you and All-Aware of all of your affairs. The closing names are not decoration: since honour is measured in hearts, only the One who knows hearts can rank people at all — which is why we cannot. Ibn Kathir adds that several scholars relied on this ayah and these hadiths as evidence that compatibility in marriage (*kafāʾah*) is not a condition of marriage contracts; the only condition required is adherence to the religion.

## Living it

Stop the joke before it leaves your mouth: you do not know whose heart weighs more with Allah. Assume the good reading of your brother's words while any good excuse remains. Leave hidden things hidden. When a conversation turns to someone absent, defend him — and if you cannot, decline to listen. Spend on your own faults the attention you were about to spend on someone else's. And when you catch yourself ranking people by colour, family or wealth, remember Bilāl giving the adhān at the Kaʿbah.

passages.title: The Bedouins' claim: Islam versus true faith
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** A delegation of desert Arabs comes to Madinah announcing, "We believe" — and Allah corrects them in front of the whole ummah for all time: you have not yet believed; say instead, "We have submitted." From that one correction the surah's closing five ayat unfold: what real faith looks like (15), Who it is that actually inspects hearts (16), whose favour is being done to whom (17), and the seal — that Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth and sees exactly what you do (18). The thread running through all five is a single claim being tested: **a tongue said one thing; a heart had not yet done it.**

This is also the end of Surah al-Hujurat. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the sequence: the surah first set out the rights of the Prophet ﷺ and the rules of how to respect and honour him, then the individual and collective rights and rules of good manners to be applied in social life. And just before this passage it was stated that the basis of honour in the sight of Allah is righteousness, which is an inner quality that Allah alone knows — so it is improper for any man to claim self-sanctification. Now at the conclusion of the surah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is reiterated that in the Hereafter good deeds will be accepted and rewarded on the basis of faith, sincere belief of the heart, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. These closing ayat drive the same nail home from the other side: since what counts is inward, no outward announcement can manufacture it.

## The occasion: a delegation from Banu Asad

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, on the authority of Imam Baghawi, that these verses came down concerning the tribe of **Banu Asad**. Some of their men arrived in Madinah during a severe drought. They were not sincere believers; they had professed Islam merely in order to demand financial help from the Muslims' *ṣadaqāt* funds — to enrich themselves and eradicate their poverty. Not being believers in the real sense, they were also unaware of Islamic injunctions and manners: they spread filth on the streets of Madinah, and in the marketplaces they increased the prices of necessary items.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists three things they did wrong, in order: **first** they made a false claim of faith in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ; **second** they wanted to deceive him; **third** they regarded their Islam as a favour to him. Their argument was: "We embraced Islam without any conflict — we did not fight against you as other tribes did for a length of time before becoming Muslims; therefore you should value us." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this a sort of disrespect toward the Messenger ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir preserves the same episode from the other end. Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bazzar recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said: Banu Asad came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Allah's Messenger! We embraced Islam, and before that the Arabs fought against you, yet we did not fight against you." The Prophet ﷺ replied that they understand but little, and that the Shaytan speaks through their words. Then, Ibn ʿAbbas says, ayah 17 was revealed — *"They regard as a favour to you that they have embraced Islam…"*

A man can be standing in Madinah, in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, saying the right words — and Shaytan can be the one moving his tongue.

## "We believe" — the word that was too big for them

**قَالَتِ ٱلْأَعْرَابُ ءَامَنَّا** — *the Bedouins say, "We believe."* Then comes the correction: **قُل لَّمْ تُؤْمِنُوا۟ وَلَٰكِن قُولُوٓا۟ أَسْلَمْنَا** — *Say: you do not believe; rather say, "We have submitted."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two words carefully. **آمَنَّا (āmannā)**, "we have come to believe," is a claim about the *heart* — about real belief by the heart. **أَسْلَمْنَا (aslamnā)**, "we have surrendered," in its literal meaning is to recite the kalimah of Islam, enter the fold of the religion and surrender — to hand yourself over outwardly. So the Qur'an does not call them liars about everything they did; it re-labels what they did. *You may say the smaller, true thing. You may not say the larger, untrue thing.* They were claiming faith falsely on the basis of their outward actions alone — and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, being devoid of the true spirit, this kind of Islam is merely superficial, not real and total. Mere verbal claim or lip-profession is meaningless if it is not supported by the heart.

Then the reason, and it is the most beautiful phrase in the passage: **وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ ٱلْإِيمَٰنُ فِى قُلُوبِكُمْ** — *for faith has not yet entered your hearts.* Faith is pictured as something that **enters**, that crosses a threshold and takes up residence in a place. And the wording is "not yet," not a flat "never." Ibn Kathir glosses the correction as *"you have not yet achieved the reality of faith."* This is a rebuke that leaves the door open.

## Not hypocrites — Muslims whose faith had not yet settled

This is where Ibn Kathir does his most important work. He states that this honourable ayah is proof that **iman is a higher grade than Islam**, according to the scholars of Ahl us-Sunnah wa'l-Jamaʿah. It is demonstrated too, he says, by the Hadith of Jibril, peace be upon him, when he questioned the Prophet ﷺ about Islam, then iman, then ihsan — thus moving from the general matter to one more specific, then even more specific.

He then brings the narration of ʿAmir bin Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas, which Imam Ahmad recorded and which Ibn Kathir says **is recorded in the Two Sahihs**. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave something to some men and gave nothing to one of them. Saʿd said, "O Allah's Messenger, you gave to so-and-so and so-and-so, but you gave nothing to so-and-so, even though he is a believer." The Prophet ﷺ answered, **"Or say, a Muslim."** Saʿd repeated his statement three times, and each time the Prophet ﷺ answered, **"Or say, a Muslim."** Then he ﷺ said: *"I might give some men and give nothing to others, even though the latter are dearer to me than the former. I do not give them things for fear that they might be thrown on their faces in the Fire."*

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion: the Prophet ﷺ made a distinction between the grade of *believer* and the grade of *Muslim*, indicating that iman is a more exclusive grade than Islam. (He adds that he treated the subject in detail, supported by evidence, at the beginning of his explanation of the chapter on Iman in Sahih al-Bukhari.)

And from this follows the merciful reading: **the Bedouins in this ayah were not hypocrites.** They were Muslims in whose hearts faith was not yet firmly established. They claimed a higher grade for themselves than the grade they had earned, and they were taught a lesson as a consequence. Ibn Kathir notes that this meaning agrees with the meaning given by **Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah**, and is the one **Ibn Jarir** preferred. A hypocrite is corrected by exposure; these men are corrected by *instruction* — told what to call themselves, and then told what would take them further.

## Two ways scholars frame "Islam" and "iman"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān approaches the same words from the angle of technical definition, and its conclusion is worth setting beside Ibn Kathir's.

It holds that "Islam" **in this verse** bears its *literal* meaning of outward submission and not the technical sense — so, on this reading, the verse does not itself show the technical difference between the two terms. Technically, **iman** refers to belief by the heart: a firm and unshakable belief in the Oneness of Allah and in His Messenger ﷺ. **Islam** stands for complete surrender and obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

But the two need to complement each other. In the Shariʿah, belief of the heart must manifest itself by performing deeds outwardly — the least degree of which is to proclaim the kalimah of Islam verbally. And outward performance of deeds is not recognised unless faith goes deep down into the heart; otherwise it would be hypocrisy. So the two remain different concepts — **iman is the inner quality of the heart that then manifests outwardly, while Islam starts out in outward actions and culminates in the inner sincere affirmation of the heart** — yet in terms of their goal they are mutually necessary and complementary. Iman without Islam is not possible, nor is Islam possible without iman.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān therefore rejects the idea that "Muslim" and "muʼmin" are antonyms or mutually contradictory concepts. In the Shariʿah it is not possible for a person to be a Muslim but not a muʼmin, or a muʼmin but not a Muslim. That split is possible only *lexically* — as with the hypocrites, who used to be treated like Muslims because of their outward obedience of Islamic injunctions, while their hearts were devoid of sincere faith, belief and affirmation. They were not believers. The commentary closes with the scholars' own seal: *Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.*

Both readings come from respected scholars, and they weight the terms differently: Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as ranking iman above Islam as two grades; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads "Islam" here in its bare lexical sense and preserves the technical inseparability of the two. What neither disputes is the ayah's demand — that the tongue's profession be backed by the heart.

## "He will not decrease anything of your deeds"

The correction in ayah 14 does not end in humiliation. It ends in an offer: **وَإِن تُطِيعُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ لَا يَلِتْكُم مِّنْ أَعْمَٰلِكُمْ شَيْـًٔا** — *if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not decrease anything in reward for your deeds.* Ibn Kathir explains it simply: **He will not decrease any of your rewards** — and he pairs it with Allah's words elsewhere, *"We shall not decrease the reward of their deeds in anything"* (52:21).

So the men who have just been told "you do not believe" are told in the same breath that the road is open and the accounting is honest. Start obeying, and not one particle of what you do will be shaved off the ledger. And the ayah closes: **إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ** — *Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.* Ibn Kathir notes for whom: **for those who repent and return to Him.** A rebuke that ends in the two names of mercy is a rebuke meant to heal.

## Ayah 15: the portrait of the real believer

Having said what these men are not, Allah paints what a believer *is* — and the word **إِنَّمَا (innamā)**, "only," makes it a restriction: *only* those are the believers, and by implication no one else.

Ibn Kathir reads **إِنَّمَا ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ** as meaning those **who have perfect faith**, and then walks through the three marks in the order the ayah gives them:

**1. They believed in Allah and His Messenger.** The starting point — the same words the Bedouins used.
